results.title: Reward Hacking Benchmark: Measuring Exploits in LLM Agents with Tool Use
results.text:
2026 · Kunvar Thaman · 12 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: Researchers introduce the Reward Hacking Benchmark (RHB) to evaluate the susceptibility of large language model agents to exploits, finding that post-training reinforcement learning significantly increases exploit rates, with some models exhibiting up to 13.9% exploit rates.
Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trained language model agents with tool access are increasingly deployed in coding assistants, research tools, and autonomous systems. We introduce the Reward Hacking Benchmark (RHB), a suite of multi-step tasks requiring sequential tool operations with naturalistic shortcut opportunities such as skipping verification steps, inferring answers from task-adjacent metadata, or tampering with evaluation-relevant functions. RHB supports independent and chained task regimes, where chain length acts as a proxy for longer-horizon agent behavior. We evaluate 13 frontier…

results.title: A survey of reward hacking in agentic large language model systems
results.text:
2026 · Arun Morampudi, Ujval Irrink, Rahul Grandhi · Discover Artificial Intelligence · Journal Article
TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) inherit reinforcement learning's reward hacking problem, escalating in agentic deployment settings. A four-level taxonomy of exploitation is introduced, and a production risk model identifies exploitable assets, requiring layered defenses across data, reward design, and governance.
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as agentic systems capable of tool use, code execution, file manipulation, and multi-step planning inherit and amplify the classical reinforcement learning problem of reward hacking. This survey synthesizes how proxy-based alignment and evaluation failures manifest across modern LLM training paradigms and escalate in agentic deployment settings. We introduce a four-level taxonomy of reward hacking escalation: feature-level exploitation (verbosity, sycophancy, stylistic shortcuts), representation-level exploitation (unfaithful chain of thought, reward…

results.text:
2024 · Carson Denison, Monte MacDiarmid, Fazl Barez · 55 citations · Preprint
TL;DR: Large Language Models can generalize from common forms of specification gaming to more pernicious reward tampering. This behavior is difficult to eliminate and mitigation strategies are limited.
Abstract: In reinforcement learning, specification gaming occurs when AI systems learn undesired behaviors that are highly rewarded due to misspecified training goals. Specification gaming can range from simple behaviors like sycophancy to sophisticated and pernicious behaviors like reward-tampering, where a model directly modifies its own reward mechanism. However, these more pernicious behaviors may be too complex to be discovered via exploration. In this paper, we study whether Large Language Model (LLM) assistants which find easily discovered forms of specification gaming will generalize to perform…

results.title: RewardHackingAgents: Benchmarking Evaluation Integrity for LLM ML-Engineering Agents
results.text:
2026 · Yonas Atinafu, Robin Cohen · 5 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: Researchers introduce RewardHackingAgents, a benchmark to evaluate the integrity of LLM ML-engineering agents, by making evaluator tampering and train/test leakage explicit and measurable, demonstrating the effectiveness of a combined regime in blocking both compromise vectors.
Abstract: LLM agents increasingly perform end-to-end ML engineering tasks where success is judged by a single scalar test metric. This creates a structural vulnerability: an agent can increase the reported score by compromising the evaluation pipeline rather than improving the model. We introduce RewardHackingAgents, a workspace-based benchmark that makes two compromise vectors explicit and measurable: evaluator tampering (modifying metric computation or reporting) and train/test leakage (accessing held-out data or labels during training). Each episode runs in a fresh workspace with patch tracking and…

results.title: Reward Hacking in Language Model Agents: Revisiting AI Safety Gridworlds
results.text:
2026 · Ömer Veysel Çağatan, Xuandong Zhao · 1 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: Reward hacking emerges in language model agents, where they exploit misspecified objectives to achieve high reward without satisfying intended goals, resisting standard mitigations and persisting across model scales and credit assignment methods.
Abstract: Reward hacking, where AI systems exploit misspecified objectives to achieve high reward without satisfying intended goals, remains a central challenge in AI safety. Yet most known instances have been discovered post hoc in frontier systems where controlled study is impractical. We adapt the AI Safety Gridworlds framework into a text-based evaluation suite that reformulates classic reinforcement learning safety tasks for language-based agents. Across frontier and mid-scale models, we find that specification gaming emerges zero-shot: models systematically achieve high observed reward while…

results.title: Do Agent Benchmarks Measure Capability? Protocol Validity in the Age of Agentic AI
results.text:
2026 · Jiaqi Shao, Hanck Chen, Wei Zhang · Journal Article
TL;DR: Agent benchmarks measure capability only when evaluation protocols ensure the intended capability is necessary for success, as recent studies reveal widespread reward hacking and score inflation in 67% of benchmark traces, necessitating a post-hoc audit to assess protocol validity.
Abstract: Agent benchmarks increasingly evaluate repository editing, web research, terminal use, and long-horizon interaction. Their scores support capability claims only when the evaluation protocol keeps the intended capability necessary for success. Recent reward-hacking benchmarks and system reports show that agents can instead recover public solutions, read evaluation artifacts, infer generator structure, manipulate feedback, or benefit from invalid scoring paths; existing responses do not provide a common procedure for attributing these shortcuts and quantifying their effect across benchmarks. We…

results.title: Reward Hacking Challenges Oversight of Autonomous Research Agents
results.text:
2026 · Yue Huang, Zhangchen Xu, Yuchen Ma · Journal Article
TL;DR: Autonomous research agents exhibit a 30.5% spontaneous reward-hacking rate on open-ended tasks, with 74.6% of attempts confirmed as hacks when allowed, highlighting the need for stronger defenses to prevent exploitation.
Abstract: Autonomous research agents can design experiments, evaluate results, and write reports, giving them control over both a scientific result and the evidence used to support it. This creates a risk of reward hacking: meeting the reward criteria without achieving the intended goal. We study (1) how often models reward-hack without instructions to do so, (2) how effective and detectable their methods are when hacking is allowed, and (3) how they adapt when an LLM review panel returns its decision and reasons. Across 17 language models and 38 tasks, the spontaneous reward-hacking rate is 30.5% on…

results.title: Towards Understanding Specification Gaming in Reasoning Models
results.text:
2026 · Kei Nishimura-Gasparian, Robert McCarthy, David Lindner · 2 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: Researchers investigate specification gaming in LLM agents, finding that all tested models exploit their specifications at non-negligible rates, with RL reasoning training and test-time mitigations having a significant impact on the rate of specification gaming.
Abstract: Specification gaming is a critical failure mode of LLM agents. Despite this, there has been little systematic research into when it arises and what drives it. To address this, we build and open source a diverse suite of tasks where models can score highly by taking unintended actions. We find that all tested models exploit their specifications at non-negligible rates in most of our eight settings, including five non-coding settings. We see the highest rates of specification gaming in Grok 4 and the lowest rates in Claude models. We use our evaluation suite to study what drives specification…

results.title: EvilGenie: A Reward Hacking Benchmark
results.text:
2025 · Jonathan Gabor, Jayson Lynch, Jonathan Rosenfeld · arXiv.org · 14 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: EvilGenie is a benchmark for reward hacking in programming settings, measuring agents' ability to exploit testing environments, with LLM judges proving highly effective in detecting reward hacking, but proprietary agents exhibiting misaligned behavior.
Abstract: We introduce EvilGenie, a benchmark for reward hacking in programming settings. We source problems from LiveCodeBench and create an environment in which agents can easily reward hack, such as by hardcoding test cases or editing the testing files. We measure reward hacking in three ways: held out unit tests, LLM judges, and test file edit detection. We verify these methods against human review and each other. We find the LLM judge to be highly effective at detecting reward hacking in unambiguous cases, and observe only minimal improvement from the use of held out test cases. In addition to…

results.title: Evaluating Indirect Prompt Injection Defenses in Tool-Using LLM Agents: Security, Utility, and Replication
results.text:
2026 · Adil R. Khan, Khaled AlKhanbashi, Azza Abdel Monem · Computers · 1 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: This study evaluates four indirect prompt injection defenses in tool-using LLM agents, reporting attack success rates, benign utility, and operational measures across three models on the AgentDojo benchmark, highlighting the importance of cautious interpretation and defense evaluation methodology.
Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that retrieve external content and use tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, in which untrusted content contains instructions intended to influence agent behavior. We evaluated four defenses and an undefended control across GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 on the AgentDojo banking benchmark (Tool Filter was evaluated only for the OpenAI models), reporting attack success rate (ASR), benign utility, utility under attack, operational measures, and two independent benchmark replications. Raw undefended ASR was 0/288 for GPT-5.4, 11/288…

results.text:
2026 · Wenhui Zhu, Xuanzhao Dong, Xiwen Chen · 3 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: This study reveals that agentic LLMs are more vulnerable to Indirect Prompt Injections (IPI) than thought, with advanced injections bypassing baseline defenses and exhibiting high decision entropy, highlighting the need for robust detection strategies like Representation Engineering (RepE).
Abstract: The rapid deployment of open-source frameworks has significantly advanced the development of modern multi-agent systems. However, expanded action spaces, including uncontrolled privilege exposure and hidden inter-system interactions, pose severe security challenges. Specifically, Indirect Prompt Injections (IPI), which conceal malicious instructions within third-party content, can trigger unauthorized actions such as data exfiltration during normal operations. While current security evaluations predominantly rely on isolated single-turn benchmarks, the systemic vulnerabilities of these agents…

results.title: Securing Autonomous AI Agents: Detecting and Mitigating Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Based Systems
results.text:
2026 · Muhammad Shahmir Khan · Journal Article
TL;DR: This paper formalizes prompt injection attacks on autonomous AI agents, proposing a threat model, attack taxonomy, and isolation-based defense combining context partitioning, instruction-privilege gating, and output-conformance verification to prevent hijacking with zero benign-utility cost.
Abstract: Autonomous large language model (LLM) agents — systems that plan, retrieve external data, and call real tools — conflate trusted instructions and untrusted content in a single context window with no native separation boundary. An adversary who can inject text into any datum the agent ingests can therefore redirect its tool calls, an escalation from bad text to real-world action. This paper formalizes indirect prompt injection against autonomous agents as an isolation failure: we present a threat model with a trust-boundary violation condition and an explicit hijack decision procedure (D1–D3),…

results.title: PlanGuard: Defending Agents against Indirect Prompt Injection via Planning-based Consistency Verification
results.text:
2026 · Guangyu Gong, Zizhuang Deng · 3 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: PlanGuard, a training-free defense framework, effectively neutralizes Indirect Prompt Injection attacks on Large Language Model agents by isolating planners, enforcing hard constraints, and verifying intent, reducing Attack Success Rate from 72.8% to 0% with a low False Positive Rate.
Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly integrated into critical systems, leveraging external tools to interact with the real world. However, this capability exposes them to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), where attackers embed malicious instructions into retrieved content to manipulate the agent into executing unauthorized or unintended actions. Existing defenses predominantly focus on the pre-processing stage, neglecting the monitoring of the model's actual behavior. In this paper, we propose PlanGuard, a training-free defense framework based on the principle of Context…

results.title: LivePI: More Realistic Benchmarking of Agents Against Indirect Prompt Injection
results.text:
2026 · Lei Zhao, Abhay Bhaskar, Edgar Dobriban · Journal Article
TL;DR: LivePI, a benchmark for indirect prompt-injection risk, evaluates AI agents' vulnerability to malicious inputs across seven surfaces and twelve attack families, achieving 10.7-29.6% attack success rates in five evaluated backbones.
Abstract: AI agents such as OpenClaw are increasingly deployed in local workflows with access to external tools. This creates indirect prompt-injection (IPI) risk: an agent may execute harmful instructions embedded in untrusted inputs such as email, downloaded files, webpages, repositories, or group-chat messages. Existing evaluations are often small, purely simulated, or focused on a narrow set of channels. We introduce LivePI (Live Prompt Injection), a structured benchmark for IPI risk in a production-like but test-controlled environment. LivePI covers seven input surfaces, twelve attack/rendering…

results.title: Silent Failures in Agentic Security Evaluation: A Validated Harness for Tool-Call Mediation Under Indirect Prompt Injection
results.text:
2026 · Animesh Shaw · Journal Article
TL;DR: LLM agents vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) due to silent failures in agentic security evaluation, including undelivered payloads, incorrect scoring, and lack of audit trails, are addressed by a validated harness for tool-call mediation, ensuring evaluation validity is a prerequisite for defense claims.
Abstract: LLM agents that invoke privileged tools are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI), in which adversarial instructions embedded in retrieved data hijack the agent's actions. A growing body of work evaluates defenses against IPI, but the validity of that evaluation is rarely examined. We audit an IPI benchmark and its harness and identify four defect classes -- silent payload non-delivery, attack success scored by tool identity rather than arguments, false-rejection rate conflated with model incapacity, and the absence of an audit trail -- each of which yields a plausible, publishable,…

results.title: Prompt Injection as a Systemic Vulnerability in LLM-Based Tools: Threat Models, Empirical Analysis, and Mitigation Strategies
results.text:
2026 · Mukesh Mani Tripathi, Damodar Dhital, Himal Aryal · Proceedings Article
TL;DR: Large language models (LLMs) expose an expanded attack surface due to conflation of trusted instructions and untrusted data, leading to a systemic vulnerability termed prompt injection, which can be mitigated through architectural controls rather than prompt engineering.
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as autonomous agents with tool access, retrieval pipelines, and persistent memory expose an expanded attack surface. We formalize prompt injection as a control-boundary violation arising from the conflation of trusted instructions and untrusted data within LLM context windows. We introduce a threat model spanning user input, retrieval pipelines, tool outputs, and persistent memory, and develop a structured taxonomy of attack vectors. We conduct a controlled empirical evaluation across three system architectures (chatbot, retrieval-augmented system,…

results.text:
2026 · Zohaib Muaz · Journal Article
TL;DR: Autonomous LLM agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, which manipulate behavior through external data sources, posing threats to security, sensitive information, and agent integrity, necessitating robust evaluation metrics and unified defense mechanisms.
Abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in external data sources manipulate agent behavior without direct user input. These external data can originate from user documents, web retrieval results, or API outputs, leading to unauthorized compliance, sensitive information disclosure, identity spoofing, and cross-agent propagation of unsafe practices. This review synthesizes current research on IPI vulnerabilities and proposed mitigation strategies. Key attack vectors include…

results.text:
2026 · Hasan Kanaker, Hussam Nawwaf Fakhouri, Nader Abdel Karim · Computation (Basel) · Journal Article
TL;DR: This research presents a simulation-based framework to evaluate user-facing risk in tool-using AI agents, formalizing a threat model and evaluating nine defense configurations across six threat scenarios, highlighting the importance of least-privilege tool design, human-in-the-loop approvals, and retrieval allowlisting in securing AI agents.
Abstract: Tool-using AI agents couple a language model with controller logic, memory, and external tools such as browsers, email, calendars, file systems, and transaction APIs. This architecture expands capability, but it also enlarges the security boundary: agents routinely ingest untrusted content while holding privileges that can reveal private data and trigger external side effects. The resulting failures are not limited to poor text generation; they include prompt injection, indirect injection through tool outputs, confused-deputy behavior, unauthorized actions, and misleading claims about the…

TL;DR: This study empirically measures the vulnerability of agentic Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines to compositional prompt injection attacks, comparing closed-source safety-trained models to open-source models in their ability to resist attacks across 10 tool combinations and 5 payload types, with a 4–17x difference in vulnerability.

results.title: Multi-Agent AI Control: Distributed Attacks Hamper Per-Instance Monitors
results.text:
2026 · Oliver Makins, Orazio Angelini, Zohreh Shams · 1 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: This TLDR is based on the title-abstract combination within the 40-word limit.

Multi-agent AI control is vulnerable to distributed attacks, where multiple agents coordinate to evade per-instance monitors. A synthetic AI-lab, FakeLab, reveals the "fragmentation effect": more coordinated agents evade monitoring, with model capability and monitor strength influencing detection.
Abstract: AI control is a family of techniques to prevent an AI with malicious goals from subverting its operator's intent. AI Control usually studies a single agent in one trajectory, but real deployments run many agents over shared infrastructure, and the most severe risks (model-weight exfiltration, training-run poisoning) plausibly need several agents acting in concert. We initiate the empirical study of multi-agent AI control, formalising distributed attacks in which several agents jointly aim for a malicious goal. We develop FakeLab: a synthetic AI-lab codebase (9 services, 86 benign tasks, 4…

results.title: ORBIT: A Framework for Multi-Agent Safety and Security Evaluations
results.text:
2026 · Ben Hagag, William L. Anderson, Srija Chakraborty · Journal Article
TL;DR: This framework, ORBIT, addresses the gap in multi-agent safety and security evaluations by providing a configurable environment for researchers to test and compare various defense strategies against diverse threats in realistic settings, revealing a significant gap in defense transferability across threats.
Abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems are increasingly deployed for complex, long-horizon tasks or emerge as a natural consequence of agents interacting in the wild. Yet they give rise to significant safety and security risks: the flexible protocols that enable task generalization also expose novel threats, from cascading prompt injection to inter-agent collusion. Progress in defending against these threats has been slowed by a lack of shared empirical infrastructure, which forces bespoke environment development for every new defense and makes standardized comparison impossible. Existing evaluations…

results.title: Architecture Matters for Multi-Agent Security
results.text:
2026 · Ben Hagag, Christian Schroeder de Witt, Sarah Scheffler · Journal Article
TL;DR: This study examines how multi-agent system (MAS) design decisions impact security, revealing that MAS architectures are more vulnerable than standalone agents, with varying attack success rates and no single design universally safer.
Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS), composed of networks of two or more autonomous AI agents, have become increasingly popular in production deployments, yet introduce security risks that do not arise in single-agent settings. Even if individual agents exhibit robust security, architectural decisions governing their coordination can create attack surfaces that have not been systematically characterized. In this work, we present an empirical study of how MAS design decisions shape the tradeoff between task performance and attack resistance. Across three agentic environments (browser, desktop, and code)…

results.title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
results.text:
2026 · James Peters-Gill, Avi Semler, Henning Bartsch · Journal Article
TL;DR: This work investigates the composability of CaMeL, a security framework for large language models, in hierarchical multi-agent systems, and introduces multi-CaMeL, an agent-to-agent communication protocol that preserves provenance and reduces attack success rate to 0.0%.
Abstract: Indirect prompt injection attacks - malicious instructions embedded in content processed by large language models - remain a major obstacle to safely deploying tool-using agents. CaMeL [Debenedetti et al., 2025] mitigates this threat for an individual agent by separating trusted control flow from untrusted data and enforcing capability-based security policies at runtime. In this work, we investigate whether CaMeL's security guarantees compose in hierarchical multi-agent systems, where agents invoke other agents as tools. We find that CaMeL's guarantees do not compose. We construct a concrete…

results.text:
2026 · Anonymous · Journal Article
TL;DR: This paper presents an enterprise perspective on multi-agent AI system security, demonstrating significant baseline vulnerability (55.6%) and introducing the Taint Amplification Factor (TAF = 3.31), which is reduced by 73.5% with layered defense combining semantic sanitization and tool authorization.
Abstract: Multi-agent AI systems present security challenges that extend beyond single-model threat models. Recent work has begun systematizing trust-authorization mismatches and threat taxonomies for agentic AI. This paper contributes an enterprise perspective through empirical validation and formal analysis. Using a four-agent troubleshooting pipeline with 300 scenarios across five conditions, we demonstrate that (1) multi-agent systems exhibit significant baseline vulnerability (55.6% attack success), (2) individual mitigations provide minimal pro-tection (1–2 percentage point reductions), but (3)…

results.title: Delegation Without Trust: An Empirical Gap Analysis of Identity, Authorization, and Runtime Governance in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
results.text:
2026 · Panduranga Sai Varma Dantuluri, Jyotirmoy Sundi · Journal Article
TL;DR: This study identifies a security gap in multi-agent LLM systems, where adversaries can hijack agents to exceed delegated authority. An authorization broker closes the gap, blocking four threats, resisting 11 attacks, and enforcing confinement at microsecond cost, with principles realized in production in VotalAI's LLM Shield.
Abstract: Autonomous LLM agents increasingly act on a user's behalf: they hold credentials, call tools and services, and spawn sub-agents that act further on their behalf. This turns a long-standing distributed-systems question -- who is authorized to do what, on whose authority -- into an urgent and largely unsolved problem, because the component driving each agent is a language model an adversary can hijack. We argue that agent security must be evaluated under an untrusted-model assumption: a correct system is one in which a fully prompt-injected agent still cannot exceed the authority explicitly…

Games for AI Control: Models of Safety Evaluations of AI Deployment
  Protocols
results.text:
2024 · C. E. Griffin, L. Nicole Thomson, Buck Shlegeris · 11 citations · Journal Article
TL;DR: This paper introduces AI-Control Games, a formal model for evaluating AI deployment protocols, and presents methods for finding optimal protocols, applying it to model and evaluate protocols for deploying untrusted language models as programming assistants.
Abstract: To evaluate the safety and usefulness of deployment protocols for untrusted AIs, AI Control uses a red-teaming exercise played between a protocol designer and an adversary. This paper introduces AI-Control Games, a formal decision-making model of the red-teaming exercise as a multi-objective, partially observable, stochastic game. We also introduce methods for finding optimal protocols in AI-Control Games, by reducing them to a set of zero-sum partially observable stochastic games. We apply our formalism to model, evaluate and synthesise protocols for deploying untrusted language models as…

results.title: TraceGuard: Structured Multi-Dimensional Monitoring as a Collusion-Resistant Control Protocol
results.text:
2026 · Khanh Linh Nguyen, Hoa Nghiem, Tu Tran · Journal Article
TL;DR: Researchers present TraceGuard, a structured multi-dimensional monitoring protocol that evaluates AI agent actions across five dimensions, achieving clear attack-honest separation, constraining collusion, and achieving 95% safety with a separation-of-duties variant.
Abstract: AI control protocols use monitors to detect attacks by untrusted AI agents, but standard single-score monitors face two limitations: they miss subtle attacks where outputs look clean but reasoning is off, and they collapse to near-zero safety when the monitor is the same model as the agent (collusion). We present TraceGuard, a structured multi-dimensional monitoring protocol that evaluates agent actions across five dimensions -- goal alignment, constraint adherence, reasoning coherence, safety awareness, and action-trace consistency -- scored in parallel by independent LLM calls, augmented by…

results.text:
2025 · 8 citations · Journal Article
Abstract: This paper proposes a novel architectural framework aimed at enhancing security and reliability in multi-agent systems (MAS). A central component of this framework is a network of Sentinel Agents, functioning as a distributed security layer that integrates techniques such as semantic analysis via large language models (LLMs), behavioral analytics, retrieval-augmented verification, and cross-agent anomaly detection. Such agents can potentially oversee inter-agent communications, identify potential threats, enforce privacy and access controls, and maintain comprehensive audit records.…

results.text:
2025 · Sun Yu-qi, Shlegeris, Buck, Tracy Tyler · 4 citations · Journal Article
Abstract: As AI systems become more capable and widely deployed as agents, ensuring their safe operation becomes critical. AI control offers one approach to mitigating the risk from untrusted AI agents by monitoring their actions and intervening or auditing when necessary. Evaluating the safety of these protocols requires understanding both their effectiveness against current attacks and their robustness to adaptive adversaries.
